The History
Walter Hines Page  ·  1855–1918

He named it Garran Hill.The Moore County life he imagined there remained largely unrealized.

He bought the land in February 1913. Named it Garran Hill. Six weeks later, Woodrow Wilson appointed him Ambassador to the Court of St. James.

He sailed for London. Into the war. Construction was supervised by his son Ralph Page, from Boston architectural plans, supported by Pinehurst builders working with Leonard Tufts.

From London, through four years of war, he wrote home about one thing.

"The farm — the farm — the farm."

Walter Hines Page  ·  The Life and Letters of Walter H. Page, Vol. I, P. 354  ·  1923

Page returned to North Carolina in failing health in December 1918. He died days after arriving, carried from the train at Aberdeen. The Moore County life he had imagined at Garran Hill remained largely unrealized.

"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?"

Co-founder of Doubleday, Page & Co. Editor of The Atlantic Monthly. A plaque in Westminster Abbey.

Garran Hill was built for a life Page never had the chance to live.

The Restoration Record  ·  1999–2001

Preserved. Restored.Redrawn.

The restoration did not make Garran Hill new. It made the house legible again.

Acquired in 1998, after the property had been vacant for approximately 14 years. Architect Thomas O'Shea prepared a full restoration plan set — 36 sheets covering elevations, floor plans, foundation, framing, portico, kitchen, primary suite, library built-ins, and reflected ceiling plans.

The architectural drawings — all 36 sheets — transfer with the property.

Everything in this entry was here the day the house opened.

The Staircase  ·  1916

The staircase has turnedthe same curve since 1916.

The Grounds
The Hollycrest Years  ·  Betty Dumaine

Horses. Hounds. Peacocks.Native hollies on every path.

Elizabeth “Betty” Dumaine purchased Garran Hill in 1959 and renamed it Hollycrest. She stewarded it until 1984. Horses in the fields. Hounds in the yard. Peacocks on the lawn. Native hollies on every path.

She named her Irish Hunter Blue Fox. He is buried somewhere on these grounds.

Someone still puts flowers there.

Blue Fox  ·  Betty Dumaine's Irish Hunter  ·  Buried on the grounds  ·  1959–1984
The Grounds  ·  4.15 Acres

The world outside these gatesdoes not exist here.

Twenty-eight irrigation zones. 130-foot well. Underground utilities throughout.

A 20-by-40 in-ground concrete pool enclosed by a brick wall with iron gates, converted to saltwater in 2022.

The Wee Cottage — a children's playhouse, one of the grounds' gentlest surprises. A small house within the larger story.

Two regulation tennis courts remain part of the estate's sporting landscape, ready for renewal.

Garran Hill  ·  At Dusk

The lights were onbefore you arrived.

Four acres. One house. Seven fireplaces. The grounds lit at the edges.

The estate at dusk is the estate at its most honest.
